All three tabs are open and confirmed. Here's your beginner sketch reference pack:

## 📌 Your reference pack (all tabs left open)

**1. Figure reference (Pinterest pin)**
- **Link:** https://www.pinterest.com/pin/1035546508122278459/
- *Figure pose reference full body | Standing pose reference woman, Standing model poses drawing reference, Anatomy photo*
- A real full-body reference photo of a person in a light leotard on a plain, neutral background — clean, uncluttered, and clear enough for a beginner to trace proportions and pose from.

**2. Background setting — 1500s English hut (source page)**
- **Link:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Thatched_Cottage
- *The Thatched Cottage* — a real, documented **16th-century (1500s) English timber-framed thatched cottage** in Carlton Husthwaite, North Yorkshire (Grade II* listed). The page has a clear photo ("The house, in 2007") showing the thatched hipped roof, timber frame, small windows, and doorway — exactly the rustic English look for a simple background.

**3. Mood reference — angry cats (Bored Panda)**
- **Exact page title:** **"40 Times People Just Had To Snap A Pic Of Their Angry, But Cute Cats"**
- (Full browser tab title: *40 Times People Just Had To Snap A Pic Of Their Angry, But Cute Cats | Bored Panda*)
- **Link:** https://www.boredpanda.com/cute-angry-cats/
- A fun collection of grumpy/irritated cat faces — great for stealing expressive "annoyed" looks (airplane ears, squinted eyes, scowls).

---

## ✏️ How they work together in one simple sketch

Combine all three into a single cozy little scene:

- **Background (the hut):** Block in the cottage first as a simple backdrop — a rectangle for the walls plus a big triangle/trapezoid for the thatched roof, a small door, and one or two tiny windows. Keep it loose and light so it reads as "setting" without stealing focus.
- **Figure (the reference):** Place your character in the foreground, using the standing-pose photo for correct body proportions and a natural stance. Since the reference is a full-body standing pose, you get a solid, easy-to-copy skeleton for your character.
- **Mood (the angry cat):** Give the character a grumpy, "annoyed cat" face — furrowed brows, narrowed/squinting eyes, a small scowl or huff, maybe arms crossed or a puffed-up defensive posture. This is what makes the drawing charming and funny.

**The resulting idea:** *A full-body character standing in front of a small 1500s English thatched cottage, wearing a comically irritated "angry cat" expression* — e.g., the person just got woken up / their tea was spilled / the cat knocked something over, and they're standing there seething. It's simple (one background shape + one figure + one expressive face), beginner-friendly, and gives you a clear, cute narrative in a single casual sketch.

Tip for a first pass: sketch the hut in light gray, build the figure from the reference with simple shapes (head, torso, limbs), then finish with the angry face — that's the part that brings the whole piece to life.
